lessons.title: Vectors, norms and cosine
lessons.intro: A vector is an ordered list of numbers read as a point or an arrow. Everything in ML, from a feature row to a word embedding, is a vector, and the first question about two of them is how alike they are.
takeaways: The dot product is length x length x cos(angle); zero means orthogonal.
Cosine removes length; normalise once and a dot product is a cosine.
L1, L2 and L-infinity measure size differently, and the choice matters for regularisation.
lessons.trap: Using raw dot products to rank by similarity when vector norms vary: long vectors win regardless of direction.

sections.heading: Length and dot product
sections.text: The L2 norm is the arrow's length. The dot product sums products of matching entries, and equals length times length times the cosine of the angle between the arrows.

sections.heading: Cosine similarity
sections.text: Divide the dot product by both lengths to keep the angle only. Doubling a vector changes its dot products but not its cosine, so cosine compares direction, which is usually what an embedding encodes.
code: cos = lambda a, b: a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

sections.heading: Norms measure different things
sections.text: L1 adds absolute values, L2 is the straight-line length, L-infinity is the largest entry. Regularisers use them because their balls have different shapes: L1 corners favour exact zeros.

lessons.title: Matrices as linear maps, and their shapes
lessons.intro: A matrix is a machine that turns vectors into vectors. Its columns say where the basis vectors land, and a matrix product is the machine you get by running one after another.
takeaways: Columns of a matrix are the images of the basis vectors.
Check (m, k) @ (k, n) -> (m, n) before running anything.
AB is not BA; (AB)^T = B^T A^T.
lessons.trap: Swapping the operands of a matmul that happens to be shape-legal both ways: it runs, and gives the wrong thing.

sections.heading: Columns are destinations
sections.text: Multiplying R by (1, 0) picks out R's first column. So a rotation, a stretch or a shear can be read straight off the matrix.

sections.heading: Shapes are the type system
sections.text: (m, k) @ (k, n) gives (m, n). Write the shapes before the code. A neural-network layer is X @ W with X (batch, in) and W (in, out).

sections.heading: Order matters
sections.text: Products are associative but not commutative, and the transpose of a product reverses the order. Backprop leans on exactly this: gradients flow through W^T.

lessons.title: Inverses, rank and solving systems
lessons.intro: Solving A x = b asks which input the map A sent to b. Whether there is exactly one answer depends on rank: how many independent directions A keeps.
takeaways: Rank is the number of independent rows (or columns); full rank means invertible.
Check the condition number before trusting a solution; regularise if it is huge.
lessons.trap: Calling `inv` on a nearly singular matrix and trusting the output: no error is raised, the numbers are just meaningless.

sections.heading: Rank counts independent directions
sections.text: If a row is a combination of others, the map flattens space and loses information. Rank less than the size means singular: no inverse, and either no solution or infinitely many.

sections.heading: Solve, do not invert
sections.text: Forming A^-1 and multiplying is slower and less accurate than a factorisation-based solve. You almost never need the inverse itself.

sections.heading: Nearly singular is the real danger
sections.text: The condition number says how much input error is amplified. A huge value means a tiny wiggle in b swings x wildly, even though the matrix is technically invertible. Ridge regression adds λI to fix exactly this.

lessons.title: Orthogonality and projections
lessons.intro: Orthogonal directions do not interfere, which is why they make clean coordinates. Projection asks for the part of a vector that lies along a direction, and it is the geometry behind least squares.
takeaways: Projection keeps the part along a direction; the residual is orthogonal.
Least squares leaves a residual orthogonal to every feature column.
Orthonormal columns: Q^T Q = I, no inverse needed.
lessons.trap: Forgetting that the projection formula needs the denominator u . u: it is only the plain dot product when u has length 1.

sections.heading: Projecting onto a line
sections.text: The component of v along u is (v . u / u . u) u. What is left over, the residual, is orthogonal to u.
code: print(p, v - p, round((v - p) @ u, 12))

sections.heading: Least squares is a projection
sections.text: Fitting y with the columns of X finds the point of the column space closest to y. The error is orthogonal to every column, so X^T (y - X w) = 0: those are the normal equations.

sections.heading: Orthonormal bases are free to invert
sections.text: If Q has orthonormal columns then Q^T Q = I, so Q^T is the inverse on its span. Rotations are the square case. Work in an orthonormal basis whenever you can.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors, SVD and PCA
lessons.intro: Most matrices rotate and bend space. Eigenvectors are directions a symmetric matrix only stretches, and the SVD is the all-purpose version that works for any matrix. PCA, LSA and low-rank compression are all the SVD in different clothes.
takeaways: Covariance matrices are symmetric positive semi-definite: real eigenvalues, none negative.
The top-k SVD is the best rank-k approximation; the error is the dropped singular values.
PCA = centre, SVD, read variance shares from s^2.
Power iteration gets the top direction with only matrix-vector products.
lessons.trap: Running PCA on uncentred data, or on features with wildly different units, and then reading the components as if they meant something.

sections.heading: Eigenvectors and the covariance matrix
sections.text: A symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. For a covariance matrix they are the principal axes and the variance along each. Because v^T C v is a variance, every eigenvalue is at least 0: the matrix is positive semi-definite.

sections.heading: SVD and low-rank approximation
sections.text: A = U S V^T with orthonormal U and V and non-negative S. Keeping only the top k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation (Eckart-Young); the error is the discarded values.

sections.heading: PCA is SVD on centred data
sections.text: Subtract each column's mean, take the SVD, and the rows of Vt are the principal directions. The share of variance of component i is s_i^2 over the sum of all s^2.

sections.heading: Power iteration finds the top direction
sections.text: Multiply a random vector by A^T A over and over, normalising each time: it converges to the top right-singular vector. It needs only matrix-vector products, which is how huge sparse matrices are handled.
